newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori builds wall of silence in crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori builds wall of silence in crisis.

text.p: When a heavily-armed group of Marxist guerrillas stormed a lavish reception at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Dec 17, the world waited to see what Peru's President Alberto Fujimori would say.
Nine days later, and with 104 VIP hostages still held by the roughly 20 gunmen, the normally publicity-seeking president has made just one terse two-minute speech on the crisis.

On the first day of the crisis the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas said Fujimori had an hour to appear at the site or they would begin killing hostages, starting with Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela.
Fujimori ignored the ultimatum and has not given an inch to the rebels since.
Even for this single-minded son of Japanese immigrants, it has been a brave stand.

In the period following his surprise 1990 election victory, Fujimori has decimated Peru's two main guerrilla groups, jailing their leaders and setting up a "faceless" courts system to try terrorists with judges who usually wear hoods.

Seen only once in public since the crisis began, shaking hands with Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, Fujimori made his first, and only, public comments four days after MRTA rebels burst onto the world's front pages with their dramatic commando-style attack.
His blunt address made it clear he was in no mood to bargain.
"The proposal is concrete: that the captors surrender their weapons to a guarantor committee and that they allow the evacuation of all of the hostages without exception," he said.
Only then, Fujimori added, would his government rule out the use of force to rescue the trapped captives.
Brief though the speech was, the president may never have spoken at all were it not for events earlier that day.

Using a two-way radio, a local television station established contact with those inside the residence, during which both Tudela and Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki urged the government to establish a channel of communication with the MRTA to negotiate an end to the crisis.

"I suspect that the president's speech was designed to steal the headlines so that the papers did not say 'Tudela demands government negotiate with MRTA'," local political commentator Pedro Planas said.

Already falling in the opinion polls, the attack on the embassy residence was a major embarrassment for Fujimori, who had repeatedly claimed his government had virtually eradicated the MRTA and the larger Shining Path guerrilla movement.
"He has lost a lot of credibility so he has to play this one to win, at all costs," Planas said.
Signalling his intention to remain above the fray, Fujimori has designated low-profile Education Minister Domingo Palermo as the government's chief negotiator.

The increasingly elusive president has spent most of his time holed up with close aides and military generals. In the first hours of the crisis, calls to emergency numbers at Government Palace from Tudela and Aoki were not answered, government sources said.
Foreign diplomats in Lima said Fujimori appeared to be determined to make up his own mind on how to handle the crisis and was not keeping them informed of his decisions.
Fujimori has not even responded to repeated pleas from hostages to reconnect water, electricity and telephone lines cut off soon after the attack.
The president has a personal and professional stake in the crisis. Although his mother and sister were released by rebels on the first night, his brother, Pedro Fujimori, remains inside.

Fujimori's hard line on the crisis has been supported at home and abroad. Initially expressing doubts over the way the hawkish president was handling the crisis, Japan swung squarely behind him following the Dec. 22 speech.
But as the standoff dragged into its ninth day, there were signs on Thursday that Peruvians were growing restless with the lack of information coming from the government.
"The president hasn't said anything," said nightwatchman David Navarro. "He should talk to the people to let them know what is going on."
